analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to sue over racial discrimination in employment, credit, contracts, and shopping.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have expanded federal civil-rights lawsuits over discrimination in economic life, never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites a Civil War-era civil rights law to cover all economic activity: making contracts, getting loans, shopping, and using online services. It lets plaintiffs win by showing race was a motivating factor in a denial, adds liability for policies with a discriminatory effect, and bans forced arbitration of these claims. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: People of color who face discrimination when applying for loans or credit, buying or leasing property, shopping in stores or online, hiring contractors, or getting hired — plus minority-owned businesses trying to win contracts or find vendors. They would gain a federal right to a jury trial, a four-year window to sue, and the ability to sue regardless of whether they had a contract with the discriminating party.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People of color facing discrimination in economic life

how_it_helps.text: The bill covers the full range of economic life — making contracts, getting loans, credit, bonding, and insurance, buying or leasing property, and being served or refused service at a store or online — and defines 'full and equal benefit' as the same treatment white citizens receive [S3].

A plaintiff would only have to show race was a 'motivating factor' in the denial, a much easier standard than the 'but for' causation the Supreme Court imposed in Comcast v. NAAOM, and the bill also bans policies whose effect is unjustifiably discriminatory, not just intentional discrimination [S3].
Standing would no longer be limited to parties or beneficiaries of a contract with the defendant, closing a loophole the Comcast case opened [S2, S3].

Pre-dispute arbitration agreements and jury-trial waivers would be unenforceable for these claims, guaranteeing a day in court before a jury, with employer and government liability for their agents' conduct and a four-year window to sue [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumer-facing businesses — retailers, lenders, insurers, landlords, tech platforms, and employers — that would face disparate-impact claims and easier causation standards, plus the arbitration industry, which would lose the forced-arbitration channel for these disputes. Some added defense costs would be passed to consumers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Retailers, lenders, insurers, landlords, and employers

drawbacks.text: The bill applies to 'pending' cases the moment it is enacted, changing the rules in lawsuits already underway, which courts and defendants would contest as retroactive [S3].

The disparate-impact standard, combined with a demanding 'substantial business necessity' defense and the bill's own broad 'economic activity' definition, would expose many neutral business practices — credit-scoring formulas, storefront security policies, online content moderation — to litigation, and defense costs tend to be passed through to all customers [S3].

Liability flows to principals and local governments for their agents' acts, and any person suffering injury in fact may sue even without a contract with the defendant, which would broaden the pool of potential litigation beyond direct victims [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — restoring a motivating-factor standard and letting victims of economic discrimination reach a jury instead of an arbitrator — addresses a real gap left by Supreme Court rulings, especially for minority borrowers and consumers who currently lack a practical remedy. The costs are real but manageable: more litigation risk for businesses and some pass-through pricing. The main design criticism is retroactive application to pending cases, which an honest supporter would acknowledge as aggressive.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee for a year and a half, got a final referral to a subcommittee on November 1, 2022, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2023 — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S5, S1].

narrative.text: Rep. Jamie Raskin introduced the bill on June 24, 2021, joined by Rep. Mondaire Jones, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S1, S5].
Fourteen Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].

The bill waited until November 1, 2022 — four months before the Congress ended — to be referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, and no further action was ever taken [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that would have faced disparate-impact liability — retailers, lenders, insurers, landlords, and employers — and the arbitration industry are better off because the bill never moved. People facing discrimination in credit, contracts, or shopping lost the stronger remedy the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Businesses facing the new liability and the arbitration industry

for.name: Rep. Jamie Raskin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reverse what it calls Supreme Court rulings that weakened federal civil-rights protections in economic life [S1, S3].

for.name: Rep. Mondaire Jones
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill's introduction as an original supporter [S1].

for.name: 14 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat [S4].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill; it sat in full committee from June 2021 until a late subcommittee referral in November 2022, with no further action [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No roll call was ever held; the bill's entire visible support was Democratic — one sponsor and 14 Democratic cosponsors with no Republican cosponsors [S4].

industries.note: The bill would let customers and job applicants sue over discriminatory effects in serving, hiring, and refusing service, with liability flowing up to the company. Businesses would bear defense costs, some passed to consumers, while discrimination victims would gain a courtroom remedy.

Denying or pricing credit, bonding, insurance, or housing would be covered economic activity, and plaintiffs would no longer need a contract with the defendant to sue. Underwriting practices could face disparate-impact challenges.
Pre-dispute arbitration agreements would be unenforceable for these civil-rights claims, removing a channel that currently routes such disputes away from public courts and juries.
Easier causation, four-year statutes of limitations, and jury rights would expand the market for representing discrimination victims. The industry's gain runs alongside the public's access to remedy.
